A QC tool that catches pipeline errors before the expensive step

A costly production stage assigns every scanned point to a paint block. QC of that step used to mean a desktop point cloud app and a lot of manual work. I built a replacement you open in a browser. It runs the same assignment first and shows the result in 3D.

  • Matches production exactly. I read the production stage line by line and matched its filters and transforms, including the settings it ignores. Paths come from the pipeline's own constants, so the tool can't drift out of step if those paths move.
  • Designed from a survey, not one example. Before designing, I checked all 315 datasets on disk. The choice of which scans to include changed one block's point count by about 20%, so the tool has no default and makes the operator choose.
  • Hover picking that's correct. With every deck loaded, the paint blocks stack on top of each other. Ray casting and volume tests both name the wrong block. So I used GPU colour picking, where each block renders a unique colour into one pixel and the depth test decides which is in front. I checked it by hiding decks one at a time at fixed pixels. After measuring that each pick re-rendered 8.46M points, I changed it to pick only when the mouse stops.
  • Pushed back on duplicate code. I was asked for a second 1,000-line script. I delivered a 188-line entry point with no logic of its own that calls the same implementation, because an earlier copy had already drifted 199 lines out of date.
Result

When a colleague's run showed an empty viewer, the tool found why: the transform config gave angles in degrees where the pipeline reads radians. With the correct transform, 3.37M points were assigned and 0.09% left unassigned. Production would have failed the same way, so the tool caught it first.

Diagnosis, audit, fix, write-up

Found a silent label corruption bug that had been live for months

Our annotation tool rejected a batch of human-labelled images, saying some labels pointed at classes that didn't exist. The pipeline had finished green.

  • I traced it to two things. The labelling vendor renumbers class IDs 1 to N on export. A refactor months earlier had deleted the step that mapped them back, and the config file was byte-identical before and after that change.
  • I found a field in each run's saved parameters that showed which code version it ran. With that I audited 96 runs and narrowed the deploy switchover to a four-week window.
  • I showed that a run broke only when the new code met a class list with a gap in its IDs. That narrowed the damage to exactly 2 runs, not the whole dataset.
  • In a separate labelling job, repeated scan IDs had created 42 blank duplicate images and stacked 16,631 duplicate labels onto 34 others. I traced it to a step that matched images by file name after throwing away their full paths.
Result

A config-only fix, with output checked byte-for-byte against a reference run. It also includes a full class mapping, so a future reorder of the classes can't silently mislabel data.

End to end: tool, validation, delivery

Counting 80,029 flanges across seven offshore platforms, with five ways to prove the count

Repainting a platform is priced per paint block, and flanges are the standard measure of how much slow work a block holds. Nobody had the numbers. The data existed in three separate places that had never been joined, and it was older than several formats the current tools assume.

  • A count that doesn't depend on the scan. A flange seen from 15 scanners gives 15 different partial views. So I pool every point of a part across all scans and use its overall centroid. That gives one fixed location per flange, however many times it was seen. A threaded sweep reads the data at 330 to 560 MB/s and caches the result, so reruns with a different transform take seconds.
  • Why "99.8% landed in a block" proves nothing. On a roughly symmetric platform, a mirrored transform also places 100% of points. So I built five independent checks. Scanner positions projected onto the plan matched to 0.000 px and 0.000 m on 5 of 7 platforms. An image-matching score showed points landing on drawn structure 4.5 to 17.3 times more often than chance. The other three checks were floor-level matching to find which CAD frame the blocks came from, clearance from each flange to its block's walls as an error bar, and a from-scratch rewrite that reproduced all seven counts exactly.
  • Configs that were wrong. The transform settings couldn't be used as written on 3 of 7 platforms, and following them gave a clean run that assigned zero flanges. One platform's blocks were 9.8 cm off because a pose was applied that shouldn't have been. Four separate measurements agreed on the fix, which moved 190 flanges. I then showed the same defect couldn't occur on the other platforms.
  • File formats that lied. Files named 0–5 looked like type IDs but were cube faces. Three platforms labelled the part-ID field as "category". Four shipped no format description at all. I validated each field by what it contained, not by its name, and required a 90% match against the parts list. Every platform scored 98.9% or higher.
Result

78,722 flanges placed in 396 paint blocks, plus per-block point clouds for visual QC. The report states its own limits: 1,153 flanges were never scanned, and 0.8–3.8% sit across two blocks. The biggest remaining risk, upstream segmentation errors, is named rather than hidden.

An auto-aligner that knows when to ask a human

Each floor plan made from a scan had to be lined up by hand with its engineering drawing. I built a solver that proposes scale and offset, refines the result, and then decides whether it can trust its own answer.

  • Proposals come from masked cross-correlation on edge maps, computed with FFTs across a range of scales. Title blocks and text are masked out, because they attract false matches.
  • Candidates are refined at higher resolution and scored by chamfer distance. The tolerance is set in metres rather than pixels, so drawings at different scales are judged the same way.
  • A candidate is auto-accepted only when two independent rankings agree by a clear margin. Everything else goes to a person, with the top candidates ready to check.
Result

On the test site: one deck auto-accepted at 2.3 px error, the right answer ranked first on another, and zero wrong answers accepted. I wrote up the cases it can't solve, such as repeating grids and symmetric structures, so reviewers know what to expect.

Migration and verification

A 1.85 TB data swap where the tools said "success" and weren't

I replaced a production point cloud dataset with re-aligned output. Almost every standard safety check turned out to be wrong.

  • The upload CLI dropped 35% of one deck's files and still exited 0. The cause was parallel composite uploads hitting a token-refresh race under heavy load.
  • The re-aligned files were exactly the same size as the old ones, so a size-based sync would have skipped all 3,021 and reported success.
  • Recursive delete permanently removes object versions even with bucket versioning on. My own verify script also printed "all checks passed" after a parsing error skipped a check.
  • On the download side, a shared copy helper held whole 1 GB objects in memory and spawned a thread pool on every call.
Result

No files lost. I now verify by object count and CRC32C, not exit codes, and take an explicit backup before any delete. Streaming downloads cut memory from 11.8 GB to 0.5 GB and raised throughput from 62 to 87 MB/s.

Root cause and fix proposal

Debugging a crashing cluster with no shell access

Pipeline stages kept showing "Crashed" on a customer cluster. Nobody on the team had exec permission. I found that was a provisioning gap and wrote the one-line fix for the project owners. Meanwhile I worked from logs and events only.

  • The autoscaler was evicting the orchestrator's own server pods, because they had no disruption budget. That caused 500s on the concurrency lease endpoint, which killed stages as they started.
  • I ruled out two convincing red herrings. The "node out of memory" message referred to one container's limit on a 504 GB node, and DNS autoscaling looked related but wasn't the cause.
  • The final failure stopped the job at 99.87%. I traced it to a credentials DaemonSet that showed 4 of 4 ready but only 1 available.
Result

A clear written diagnosis and infra fix, not a code change. Because the job keeps a resume ledger, only the 64 missing tasks needed to rerun.

Headless CAD-to-scan alignment

FFT phase correlation and trimmed ICP in Open3D, with a known-shift self-test because a flipped sign still looks right. Showed the usual fit metric overstated error: 7.1 cm point-to-point against a true 2.7 cm point-to-plane.

Rebuilt a CAD extraction config from its output

The only config on disk was stale. I reverse-engineered one that reproduces an 85,016-element asset list byte-for-byte, checked by running the pipeline and diffing the output.

Regex rules for 743k CAD tag names

Ordered rules from specific to generic, tested against every unique name, for a model whose naming is inconsistent. Revised after a round of QC feedback.

Caught a checklist that failed correct builds

A QC step expected a file that a newer branch had replaced. File timestamps showed which build wrote what. I sent it to the branch owner instead of hand-writing the file.

Working method

How I ship with AI without shipping slop

I build with Claude Code every day. It lets me go from a question to working code quickly. These are the habits that keep the output correct.

Measure before claiming

Every result above was checked against data, by byte-for-byte diff, object count, checksum or a reference run. A green pipeline or an exit code of 0 isn't evidence on its own.

Tests with known answers

Before trusting a solver I give it a case I built, such as a synthetic shift or a rewrite from scratch that must match. I test UI changes in a real browser with headless Chrome, which is how I caught a search highlight that couldn't be seen.

Refuse, don't guess

Configs and docs were wrong more than once above. When an input is ambiguous my tools stop and say why, rather than picking a default that silently changes every result. I check behaviour against the source code, not the docs.

Keep what was learned

I keep more than 20 short notes of verified gotchas and decisions, so each new session starts from facts already checked. Several of these fixes had been hit before and forgotten.
